The '''Hopkins statistic''' (introduced by Brian Hopkins and [[John Gordon Skellam]]) is a way of measuring the [[cluster tendency]] of a data set.<ref>{{Cite journal
  | title = A new method for determining the type of distribution of plant individuals
  | last1 = Hopkins | first1 = Brian
  | last2 = Skellam | first2 = J.G.
  | journal = Annals of Botany
  | volume =18
  | number = 2
  | pages = 213–227
  | year = 1954
  | publisher = Annals Botany Co
| doi = 10.1093/oxfordjournals.aob.a083391 }}</ref> It belongs to the family of sparse sampling tests. It acts as a [[Statistical hypothesis testing|statistical hypothesis test]] where the [[null hypothesis]] is that the data is generated by a [[Poisson point process]] and are thus uniformly randomly distributed.<ref name="banerjee04">{{Cite book
 | last = Banerjee | first = A.
 | title = 2004 IEEE International Conference on Fuzzy Systems (IEEE Cat. No.04CH37542)
 | chapter = Validating clusters using the Hopkins statistic
 | pages = 149–153
 | doi = 10.1109/FUZZY.2004.1375706
 | year = 2004
| volume = 1
 | isbn = 0-7803-8353-2
 | s2cid = 36701919
 }}</ref> If individuals are aggregated, then its value approaches 1, and if they are randomly distributed along the value tends to 0.5.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Aggarwal|first=Charu C.|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-14142-8|title=Data Mining|date=2015|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-14141-1|location=Cham|pages=158|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-14142-8|s2cid=13595565 }}</ref>

==Preliminaries==

A typical formulation of the Hopkins statistic follows.<ref name="banerjee04"/>
:Let <math>X</math> be the set of <math>n</math> data points.
:Generate a random sample <math>\overset{\sim}{X}</math> of <math>m \ll n</math> data points sampled without replacement from <math>X</math>.
:Generate a set <math>Y</math> of <math>m</math> uniformly randomly distributed data points.
:Define two distance measures,
::<math>u_i,</math> the minimum distance (given some suitable metric) of <math>y_i \in Y</math> to its nearest neighbour in <math>X</math>, and
::<math>w_i,</math> the minimum distance of <math>\overset{\sim}{x}_i \in \overset{\sim}{X}\subseteq X</math> to its nearest neighbour <math>x_j \in X,\, \overset{\sim}{x_i}\ne x_j.</math>

==Definition==
With the above notation, if the data is <math>d</math> dimensional, then the Hopkins statistic is defined as:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cross |first1=G.R. |last2=Jain |first2=A.K. |title=Measurement of clustering tendency |chapter=MEASUREMENT OF CLUSTERING TENDENCY**Research supported in part by NSF Grant ECS-8007106 |journal=Theory and Application of Digital Control |date=1982 |pages=315–320 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-08-027618-2.50054-1|isbn=978-0-08-027618-2 }}</ref>

<math>
H=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^m{u_i^d}}{\sum_{i=1}^m{u_i^d}+\sum_{i=1}^m{w_i^d}} \, </math>

Under the null hypotheses, this statistic has a Beta(m,m) distribution.
